Confidence Interval for the Coefficient of Variation

Source: R/ci_cv.R
ci_cv.Rd

Computes the confidence interval for the population coefficient of variation, the standard deviation relative to the mean, from the noncentral t distribution, so that variability can be reported on a scale that is free of the measurement units. The interval is exact under normality and is not robust to departures from it (see Details).

Usage

ci_cv(
  cv = NULL,
  mean = NULL,
  sd = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  alpha_lower = NULL,
  alpha_upper = NULL
)

Arguments

cv

Sample coefficient of variation, the sample standard deviation divided by the sample mean, given with N. Must be positive.

mean

Sample mean; must be positive. It is given with sd and N.

sd

Sample standard deviation (square root of the unbiased estimate of the variance). Must be positive.

N

Total sample size, given with cv or with mean and sd. Must exceed 1; it need not be a whole number.

data

Numeric vector of at least two finite scores, given in place of the summary statistics: the coefficient of variation and the sample size are taken from it.

conf_level

Desired confidence level (1-Type I error rate). A level above .999999998, whose tail areas are below 1e-9, is refused

alpha_lower

The lower tail area. An omitted confidence level yields to supplied tail areas; an explicit level must agree with them.

alpha_upper

The upper tail area, supplied together with alpha_lower. The table records the coverage, 1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper, as its level and, when the two tail areas differ, the areas themselves, which the line beneath the printed table, results_sentence, and the alpha_lower and alpha_upper columns of tidy() state; with a tail area of 0 the interval is a one-sided confidence bound. A nonzero tail area below 1e-9 is refused (see "Small tail areas" in ci_nc_t).

Value

A 4-row data.frame with columns term, value, prob_less, and prob_greater. The rows are ordered so the two point estimates sit between the confidence limits: "ci_lower" (lower confidence limit on the coefficient of variation), "cv" (the sample coefficient of variation), "cv_unbiased" (the nearly unbiased estimate, \((1 + 1/(4 N))\) times the sample value; see cv), and "ci_upper" (upper confidence limit). The prob_less and prob_greater columns hold the requested tail areas: alpha_lower and 1 - alpha_lower at the lower limit, and 1 - alpha_upper and alpha_upper at the upper limit, also when the upper limit is infinite. They are NA for the point-estimate rows.

Details

The interval. For a random sample of \(N\) scores from a normal population with a positive mean, \(\sqrt{N} / k\), where \(k = s / M\) is the sample coefficient of variation, has a noncentral t distribution on \(N - 1\) degrees of freedom whose noncentrality parameter is \(\sqrt{N} / \kappa\), with \(\kappa = \sigma / \mu\) the population coefficient of variation (Johnson & Welch, 1940; Kelley, 2007, Equations 5 to 8; McKay, 1932). The function finds the confidence limits for the noncentrality parameter (ci_nc_t) and divides \(\sqrt{N}\) by each: the lower limit for \(\kappa\) comes from the upper limit for the noncentrality parameter, and the upper limit from the lower.

Normality. The interval is exact when the scores are a random sample from a normal distribution with a positive mean: its coverage is then the stated level at every sample size. It is not robust to departures from normality, and a larger sample does not repair it, because the distribution that is inverted is that of a normal sample whatever its size. In simulations of a nominal 95 percent interval, with 10,000 samples in each condition (population coefficients of variation of .3 and .5, sample sizes of 30 and 200), coverage was .81 to .85 for Laplace data, .90 to .94 for lognormal data, and .96 to .97 for gamma data, where it was .945 to .951 for normal data, the stated level within the error of the simulation. For the Laplace and the lognormal data it was lower at 200 than at 30. A large-sample interval that does not assume normality follows from the asymptotic normal distribution of \(k\) (Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2018, Equations 29 to 33). It needs a large sample: with 400,000 samples in each of the same conditions it covered .806 to .905 at \(N = 30\) and .894 to .942 at \(N = 200\), below the stated level in every condition, normal data included. The function does not compute it.

An infinite upper limit. The upper limit is infinite when \(\sqrt{N} / k\) is at most the 1 - alpha_upper quantile of the central t distribution on \(N - 1\) degrees of freedom, which happens when the sample coefficient is large for the sample size. The lower confidence limit of the noncentrality parameter is then not positive: at that tail area the data do not rule out a population mean of zero, and no finite coefficient of variation bounds the interval above. The infinite limit is part of the exact interval. Over repeated samples from a normal population with a positive mean, the interval covers the population coefficient with the stated probability, counting the intervals that are bounded above and those that are not. In 20,000 simulated samples with a population coefficient of .8 and \(N = 6\), the upper limit of the 95 percent interval was infinite in 31 percent and coverage was .952; with a coefficient of .5 and \(N = 5\) it was infinite in 9 percent and coverage was .948. The stated level describes all of the intervals together and neither kind alone (computed from the noncentral t distribution, coverage is .92 and .73 among the intervals with an infinite limit and .96 and .97 among the others). Nothing is signaled for an infinite limit, and the prob_less and prob_greater columns hold the requested tail areas there as at a finite limit. A sample whose mean is not positive has no interval and is refused; with a population coefficient of .5 or less and five or more scores the probability of such a sample is below .00001. Where such samples are not rare, coverage among the samples that have an interval is somewhat above the stated level: it is .962 for a 95 percent interval with a coefficient of 1 and \(N = 5\), where 1.3 percent of samples have a mean that is not positive. Of the 20,000 samples with a coefficient of .8 above, 25 had such a mean, and the figures given describe the other 19,975.

References

Johnson, N. L., & Welch, B. L. (1940). Applications of the non-central t-distribution. Biometrika, 31(3–4), 362–389. doi:10.1093/biomet/31.3-4.362

Kelley, K. (2007). Sample size planning for the coefficient of variation from the accuracy in parameter estimation approach. Behavior Research Methods, 39(4), 755–766. doi:10.3758/BF03192966

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 3 on confidence intervals for effect sizes.)

McKay, A. T. (1932). Distribution of the coefficient of variation and the extended t distribution. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, 95(4), 695–698.

Examples

# Fifteen scores from a normal population with a mean of 5 and a
# standard deviation of 1, whose coefficient of variation is .20.
set.seed(113)
x <- rnorm(15, mean = 5, sd = 1)

# The interval from the scores, from their mean and standard deviation,
# and from the sample coefficient itself: three routes to one interval.
ci_cv(data = x)
#>  term        value prob_less prob_greater
#>  ci_lower    0.150 0.025     0.975       
#>  cv          0.207 <NA>      <NA>        
#>  cv_unbiased 0.210 <NA>      <NA>        
#>  ci_upper    0.335 0.975     0.025       
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
ci_cv(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x), N = 15)
#>  term        value prob_less prob_greater
#>  ci_lower    0.150 0.025     0.975       
#>  cv          0.207 <NA>      <NA>        
#>  cv_unbiased 0.210 <NA>      <NA>        
#>  ci_upper    0.335 0.975     0.025       
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
ci_cv(cv = sd(x) / mean(x), N = 15)
#>  term        value prob_less prob_greater
#>  ci_lower    0.150 0.025     0.975       
#>  cv          0.207 <NA>      <NA>        
#>  cv_unbiased 0.210 <NA>      <NA>        
#>  ci_upper    0.335 0.975     0.025       
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# Unequal tail areas, with .01 below the interval and .04 above it.
ci_cv(data = x, alpha_lower = .01, alpha_upper = .04)
#>  term        value prob_less prob_greater
#>  ci_lower    0.142 0.010     0.990       
#>  cv          0.207 <NA>      <NA>        
#>  cv_unbiased 0.210 <NA>      <NA>        
#>  ci_upper    0.316 0.960     0.040       
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95% (unequal tail areas: 0.01 below the lower limit, 0.04 above the upper limit)
